title: Bucket training twin lambs
subtitle: Getting two lambs onto the bottle and eventually onto a bucket feeder.
excerpt: When a ewe cannot feed twin lambs adequately, or when a lamb is orphaned, bucket or bottle feeding keeps it alive and growing. The transition from bottle to a self-service bucket feeder reduces the labour demand significantly. Getting two lambs onto the same bucket without one dominating the other is the main management challenge.
sourceNotes: AHDB Beef and Lamb, Lamb Survival and Management (2021). Practical Sheep Farming (British Sheep Dairying Association, 2020). John Seymour, Complete Self-Sufficiency (1976), sheep chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: The first milk from a ewe after lambing, dense with antibodies. Lambs must receive at least 200 ml within the first 6 hours of life.
A bucket fitted with a teat that allows lambs to feed at will. The bucket holds cold milk replacer, which does not ferment as quickly as warm, reducing the number of refills needed.

content.text: The first priority with any new lamb is

. A lamb that has not had colostrum within 6 hours is at high risk; even if its ewe cannot provide enough, use frozen ewe colostrum, cow colostrum, or a commercial colostrum substitute. Never start a lamb on milk replacer before colostrum.
Warm colostrum or milk replacer to body temperature (38 to 39 C). Test on your wrist; it should feel warm but not hot.

Hold the lamb in a natural suckling position (supported upright, not on its back). Gently open the lamb's mouth and offer the teat. Most lambs latch instinctively once they have the teat correctly positioned.
Feed 50 ml per kg bodyweight every 4 hours in the first 24 hours. A 4 kg lamb needs 200 ml per feed, 6 times per day.
Transitioning to cold ad-lib bucket feeding
From day 3 to 5, most lambs can begin to learn the
. Cold milk replacer (4 to 8 C) slows fermentation, reduces overeating, and cuts the labour to one or two bucket refills per day.
Fill the bucket with cold milk replacer mixed according to the manufacturer's rate. Fix the bucket at a comfortable height: the teat should sit just above snout level when the lamb stands naturally.
Show each lamb the teat by dipping it briefly in warm milk and guiding the lamb's snout to it. Some lambs learn within 10 minutes; others need 2 to 3 sessions over 2 days.
With twin lambs, position the bucket so both can access a teat simultaneously. Observe that both are feeding; a larger or more assertive twin can prevent the smaller one from accessing the teat.

Lambs can be weaned from milk replacer at 6 to 8 weeks of age, provided they are eating a minimum of 200 to 250 g of lamb starter pellets per day. Reduce milk access over 5 to 7 days rather than cutting off abruptly.

attrs.cue: Lamb has a bloated abdomen and is uncomfortable after a feed
attrs.cause: Overfeeding or too-warm milk causing abnormal rumen fermentation; or white muscle disease
attrs.fix: Reduce the amount per feed. Ensure the lamb is not bolting large quantities at once. Persistent bloat with a stiff-legged gait may be white muscle disease (selenium deficiency); call the vet.

attrs.cue: Smaller twin not gaining weight despite access to the bucket
attrs.cause: Being displaced from the teat by the larger twin
attrs.fix: Temporarily separate the twins for three feeds per day, offering the smaller one individual access to the teat. Once the smaller lamb is feeding confidently, re-introduce them together.
